title: V3-8 — Fire Science and Egress: Buying Minutes
summary: Buildings can't be fireproof; they're designed to fail slowly and predictably so people get out. Everything in fire code buys minutes somewhere: detect early, suppress before flashover, contain in compartments, evacuate through counted-and-measured paths. PLAIN: the design goal is time. PRO: flashover, ratings and penetrations, occupant load, two remote exits, defend-in-place.

sections.heading: Flashover and the strategy
sections.body: PLAIN: A fire grows in a room until FLASHOVER — the moment radiant heat ignites everything at once, often just 3–8 minutes in a furnished room — after which nobody survives inside it. So the strategy is a relay of minutes: detect early (alarms), suppress early (sprinklers exist mainly to PREVENT flashover, and they win overwhelmingly), contain (compartments), evacuate (egress). PRO: 'flashover,' 'fuel load,' 'the sprinkler controlled it to a one-head fire' — the phrase that describes most sprinklered-building fires.

sections.heading: Compartments, ratings, and the holes
sections.body: PLAIN: Rated walls and floors are TIMERS — a '1-hour wall' holds fire back for about an hour of standard test fire. But the rating is only as good as its weakest hole: every pipe, duct, and cable through a rated wall needs FIRESTOPPING, and doors in rated walls are rated, self-closing, and never wedged open. The condos live on this — unit separations, protected stairs, shafts. PRO: 'fire-resistance rating,' 'protect the penetrations,' 'self-closers,' 'draftstopping/fireblocking' in concealed spaces. The inspector's flashlight goes straight to the penetrations — so should your QC, at every close-up.

sections.heading: Egress in one breath
sections.body: PLAIN: From any point, a person must reach safety within a limited travel distance, through paths wide enough for the crowd, with TWO separate ways out — separated enough that one fire can't block both. Doors swing with the flow for crowds; exit lights work in blackout; stairs are the choke point and sized like it. Assembly spaces — your sports bar, beach club: crowds plus alcohol — get the strictest numbers, and OCCUPANT LOAD (computed from area, not chosen by marketing) drives everything: the sports bar's legal capacity is an egress calculation. Senior living adds the hard truth that occupants evacuate slowly or not at all: more compartmentation, wider doors, sprinklers non-negotiable — 'defend in place.' PRO: 'means of egress,' 'common path of travel,' occupant load factors ~15 sf/person unconcentrated assembly / 7 net concentrated; travel distance ~200 ft / 250 sprinklered; two exits above ~49 occupants; egress width ~0.2 in/person stairs, 0.15 doors.

quiz.teach: Sprinklers aren't primarily for extinguishing — they're for interrupting the growth curve.
quiz.prompt: Why do sprinklers 'exist mainly to prevent flashover'?

choices.text: Flashover — everything igniting at once, often 3–8 minutes in — is the survivability cliff; a sprinkler head opening early keeps the fire small and the room survivable, which is why sprinklered fires so often end as 'controlled by one head'
choices.why: Correct. The sprinkler's job is to break the growth curve before the cliff — extinguishment is a bonus; time is the product.

choices.text: They extinguish fires completely before the department arrives
choices.why: Often they merely CONTROL — which is the point: a controlled pre-flashover fire is an inconvenience; a post-flashover room is a fatality scene.

choices.text: They protect the structure from heat damage
choices.why: Structural protection is a side benefit — the design driver is keeping the ROOM survivable during the minutes people need.
Insurers discount them because of the flashover math, not the other way around.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: a room fire has a countdown to the moment everything burns at once; the sprinkler stops the clock. PRO: 'suppress pre-flashover; sprinklers win overwhelmingly; defend-in-place strategies lean on them absolutely.' (V3-8)

quiz.teach: Penetration hunting: rated assemblies fail at their holes.
quiz.prompt: The kitchen designer routes a grease duct through the rated corridor wall with a plastic sleeve. Name the violations.

choices.text: Two: the penetration breaches the rated wall without a listed firestop system, and a GREASE duct — the building's highest-fire-risk duct — gets special enclosure/rating rules of its own that a plastic sleeve mocks twice over
choices.why: Correct. Any unprotected penetration voids the wall's timer; grease ducts (kitchen fires' favorite highway) carry their own enclosure requirements on top.

choices.text: One: plastic isn't allowed in commercial kitchens
choices.why: The material is the least of it — the WALL's rating is breached, and the DUCT's own protection rules are ignored. Two systems violated, not one product.

choices.text: None, if the duct has a damper somewhere
choices.why: Dampers are part of listed penetration solutions in specific configurations — and often prohibited in grease ducts specifically (grease + closing damper = trapped fire). 'Somewhere' is not a system.

choices.text: It's the fire inspector's problem to catch
choices.why: It's your QC's problem to catch at rough-in, when it costs a re-route — the inspector catching it at commissioning costs the OC date.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the fire wall is a dam, and every unsealed pipe hole is a hole in the dam — and the greasy duct is the worst possible thing to pass through unprotected. PRO: 'listed firestop systems at every penetration; grease duct enclosure per its own rules; penetration QC at every close-up.' (V3-8, S7)

quiz.teach: Occupant load is computed, and everything downstream recalculates from it.
quiz.prompt: A layout revision adds a mezzanine to the sports bar. What recalculates?

choices.text: The chain: added area → added occupant load (area ÷ load factor) → required egress width → possibly a second stair → sprinkler and alarm design → and the M11 change-cost multiplier on all of it
choices.why: Correct. Occupant load is the root variable — touch the area and every egress quantity downstream re-derives, at whatever design stage you've reached (and its multiplier).

choices.text: Just the seat count on the license
choices.why: The license number IS the egress calculation's output — you can't revise the answer without re-running the chain that produced it.
Calling occupied space storage until the fire marshal visits is a strategy with a short shelf life and your OC attached to it.
Those too (V3-1's tributary math) — but the life-safety chain is the one that can demand a second STAIR, which is the expensive surprise.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: more floor means more people means wider ways out — maybe a whole new stair. PRO: 'occupant load drives egress width drives exit count; recalculate the chain before approving the render.' The sports bar's capacity is an egress calc, not a marketing choice. (V3-8, M11)

mathProblems.title: The sports bar's legal capacity
mathProblems.context: Occupant load = floor area ÷ load factor (sf per person). This number — not marketing's — is the bar's capacity, and every egress quantity derives from it. Round up.

decisionPoints.title: Commissioning week goes sideways
decisionPoints.scenario: Fire alarm and sprinkler acceptance tests on Condo Building 2 fail on sequence-of-operations — dampers and door releases don't respond to the right zones in the right order. The fire authority's next available re-test slot is five weeks out unless someone begs. Closings are scheduled against this building's OC in three weeks. The alarm sub says the fix is 'a week of programming.'

options.label: Treat it as the revenue emergency it is: alarm sub on nights to fix and pre-test with a full self-witnessed dry run, personal call to the authority for a cancellation slot, buyers' attorneys notified of a POSSIBLE two-week slip now rather than a certain surprise later
options.outcome: The dry run is what earns the early re-test — authorities re-prioritize applicants who demonstrably won't waste the visit. The early notice to buyers converts a breach conversation into a scheduling one. Maybe you claw back three of the five weeks; all of them were on the table only because you moved today.

options.label: Take the five-week slot and tell buyers when it's certain
options.outcome: The OC slips five full weeks — the sub's week of programming plus four weeks of queue you never contested — and buyers learn of the slip at maximum lateness with minimum goodwill. Every week is general conditions plus interest plus trust.

options.label: Pursue a temporary/partial occupancy for floors away from the affected zones
options.outcome: Sometimes available, always conditional — and life-safety systems are BUILDING systems, so partial occupancy against an alarm that fails sequence testing is a hard ask that spends authority goodwill you'll want for the re-test. Explore it, but as a parallel path, not the plan.

decisionPoints.debrief: Life-safety commissioning gates the OC and the OC gates revenue — which makes a failed acceptance test a financial event measured in weeks. The response is a war room, not a queue position: fix fast, PROVE it's fixed before the authority returns, and tell the money side early. This is why S7 booked the authorities weeks ahead — and why the sequence-of-operations gets pre-tested before they ever arrive. (V3-8, S7, M14)
